facts.claim: The album Baby was recorded in September and November 2012 at Magpie Cage in Baltimore, MD. J. Robbins engineered it, Justin Fogleman assisted, and Dan Coutant mastered it.

Discogs credits production of Baby to Born Without Bones and J. Robbins. It also lists Jim Creighton on bass, Patrick Murphy on drums, Jonathan Brucato on guitar, and Scott Ayotte on guitar and vocals. Robbins is credited with slide guitar, tambourine and shaker on some tracks, and Shawna Potter with vocals on 'Bad Habit'.
Scott Ayotte said he wrote the song 'Baby' first. The rest of the album's songs were then about relationships, love and heartbreak, and he noted that many people call their partners 'baby'.
Ayotte said the band had never played 'Baby' live when they recorded it for the album. He called it almost a meme song now and said it was the song that started that.
Ayotte said Pat Murphy drummed on Baby and Young at the Bend, and on a couple of songs on Say Hello.
Ayotte said he was 21 when they recorded Baby and that the band didn't really know what they were doing.
The band said they found a lot of common ground in taste with J. Robbins. Robbins also showed them music while they made the record.
Ayotte called Baby a heartbreak record and said it is when the group really became a band and developed its sound.

Baby was self-released in 2013. Born Without Bones signed to Pure Noise Records in 2021 and issued the Pictures of the Sun EP, which re-recorded songs including 'Baby'. In 2023 they toured for the album's 10th anniversary.
Born Without Bones started as a solo project by Scott Ayotte. Guitarist Jonathan Brucato and bassist Jim Creighton later joined, and the band is from Milford, Massachusetts.

research.lineage: The band is rooted in the Massachusetts DIY punk scene and mixes 90s alternative guitars and hooks with heartland singer-songwriter storytelling, and sources also tag it as midwest emo.

draft:
**Baby** opens with an ultimatum: "You're killing me so finish me off or spare me." Then Born Without Bones swerves into something smaller and harder to bear. Scott Ayotte starts taking attendance in a house he's no longer welcome in. Where's Nicole? Is Priscilla ordering Chinese? Is Wayne working through the wine bottles everyone brought? It's the jealousy of someone picturing a party that goes on fine without them. The details are so ordinary they sting, because ordinary is exactly what he's lost.

The memories come in the same plain register: sex on the living room floor every Sunday, the smell of a log cabin, small hands reaching for his. Then the line where it curdles: "I wonder what they're clasped around now." It reads as tenderness and works as suspicion. He can't think about her hands without imagining someone else holding them. Later, a bed that sinks in the middle, a mismatch of bodies, waking up covered in lint. Ayotte keeps reaching for physical evidence, as if proving the closeness was real might bring it back.

What keeps the song honest is that he doesn't only grieve. "But I don't miss not hearing my name" admits the relationship was starving him too, that he wanted more and kept getting the same. Then he folds anyway: "You've got me now." Clear-eyed and hopelessly hooked sit in the same verse, and neither wins. The last stretch of lyrics goes big ("I lived and died," a "meaningless life"), the way heartbreak does at 21, which is how old Ayotte says he was when the band cut the record.

The arrangement holds back to start. A fingerpicked acoustic pattern circles under a clean, sustained electric chord and a bass that sticks to root notes. The tempo is moderate and the groove is relaxed. Ayotte sings clear and mid-range, alone, with no harmonies to soften it. Then the drums kick in with a driving beat, and his delivery moves from melodic to belted. It's the midwest emo move by way of Massachusetts DIY punk: a quiet confession that can't stay quiet, with 90s alternative guitars underneath and heartland storytelling in the specifics.

Ayotte says he wrote "Baby" before anything else on the album, and the band had never played it live when they tracked it with J. Robbins at Magpie Cage in Baltimore in 2012. He's called it almost a meme song now. They re-recorded it in 2021 for the Pictures of the Sun EP, and toured the album's tenth anniversary in 2023.

It sticks because it asks the question you're ashamed to ask after a breakup, what their hands are holding now, and then lets you shout it.
